new_statements.quote: The stress is usually noted at the end of the nominal and the verbal stems. The postpositions, case formants and the personal endings of the verb are in most instances unstressed. Multisyllabic words can also have a secondary stress. Phonological-relevant tone oppositions have not been noticed. But in a number of words tones have been observed. || [Edel'man 1999: 90] Ударение преимущественно силовое, падает на исход основы имени и глагола. Послелоги, падежные окончания и личные окончания глагола в большинстве форм безударны. Многосложные слова имеют второстепенное ударение. Тоновые оппозиции не прослежены, хотя наблюдаются отдельные слова с определенными тоновыми контурами.
new_statements.translation: (1999 Russian:) Stress is predominantly dynamic (expiratory) and falls on the end of the stem of the noun and of the verb. Postpositions, case endings and the personal endings of the verb are unstressed in most forms. Polysyllabic words have a secondary stress. Tonal oppositions have not been traced, although individual words with definite tonal contours are observed.
new_statements.citation: Edelman, D. I. 1983. The Dardic and Nuristani Languages (Languages of Asia and Africa). Moscow: Nauka Publishing House, Central Department of Oriental Literature. Section 'Katarkalai (Wotapuri)', Phonetics.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dynamic stress on the final syllable of the (nominal or verbal) stem; inflectional material after the stem (case endings, postpositions, verbal person endings) is normally unstressed, so stress is stem-final rather than word-final. No phonemic tone established, though some words show tonal contours.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Polysyllabic words 'can also have' (1983) / 'have' (1999) a secondary stress; position not stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged with 'usually' / 'in most instances' / 'в большинстве форм'; no specific exceptional classes named. Long vs short vowels phonemic; some words with observed tones.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement framed morphologically (stem vs endings/postpositions); based on Buddruss's 1955-56 field transcriptions of Katarqala speech as compiled by Edelman, not on Edelman's own fieldwork. Language now presumed extinct or nearly so.
new_statements.identity_note: Edelman's sketches use the name 'Katarkalai (Wotapuri)' and rest on Buddruss's material from Katarqala village (the Wotapur variety was already moribund/extinct by the 1950s); same language as Glottolog wota1240 / ISO wsv, no separate dialect code.

sources.note: p. 151: 'The stress is usually noted at the end of the nominal and the verbal stems. The postpositions, case formants and the personal endings of the verb are in most instances unstressed. Multisyllabic words can also have a secondary stress. Phonological-relevant tone oppositions have not been noticed. But in a number of words tones have been observed.' Also p. 43 (general chapter) lists Katarkalai among languages with 'phonologically relevant syllable-tone oppositions'. Sketch compiled from Buddruss 1960 (cited [Buddruss 4] in the section head).

sources.note: p. 90, sec. 5.1.0: stress is predominantly dynamic and falls on the end of the nominal and verbal stem; postpositions, case endings and verbal personal endings are mostly unstressed; polysyllables have secondary stress; tone oppositions not traced though some words show definite tonal contours; 5.1.1 syllable structure not studied. (Image-only PDF; pp. 89-91 scanned with tesseract rus at 300 dpi and read from renders.)
